title: An Analysis of NYC’s Vision Zero Program
text:
Vision Zero in New York City
Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death and injury in New York City (NYC). In 2014, the city adopted the Vision Zero (VZ) framework, a comprehensive strategy to eliminate all traffic-related fatalities. The program is built on the principle that traffic deaths are preventable and uses a multi-faceted approach, including infrastructure redesign, lower speed limits, and public awareness campaigns. This analysis evaluates the impact of nine distinct street-level interventions implemented between 2013 and 2023 on pedestrian casualties.



Citywide Pedestrian Casualty Trends
The plot below shows the total annual count of pedestrian casualties (deaths and injuries) across the 9,562 unique intersections included in our study sample. A notable drop is visible in 2020, likely corresponding to changes in traffic patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic.











Vision Zero Implementation Timeline
The Vision Zero program was rolled out in a staggered fashion, with different intersections receiving treatments in different years. The chart below illustrates the number of intersections in our sample that received their first major VZ intervention in each year of the study period (2015-2021). This excludes the citywide speed limit reduction, which was applied to nearly all intersections in 2014.











Impact of VZ Interventions on Pedestrian Safety
We used a negative binomial regression model to estimate the effect of each of the nine interventions on the annual count of pedestrian casualties, controlling for factors like traffic volume and population density. The results, presented as Incidence Rate Ratios (IRR), are shown below. An IRR below 1.0 indicates a reduction in casualties (a protective effect), while an IRR above 1.0 suggests an increase.
